editorial.headline: General Building Cleaning: Nationally Open, Bali Closed to PMA
editorial.standfirst: This activity spans routine cleaning across buildings and premises—open nationally to foreign investment, but blocked for PMA registration in Bali.
editorial.body:
General building cleaning is the everyday upkeep of buildings and their connected spaces. It covers routine cleaning for offices, houses and apartments, factories, shops and shopping premises, institutions, other business and professional locations, and multi-unit residential buildings. The centre of gravity is interior work: the cleaning that keeps rooms, shared spaces and occupied premises usable. Related exterior tasks may also fall within the activity where they remain part of the building-cleaning assignment, such as cleaning windows or building corridors.

The boundary is practical rather than decorative. This is a general-cleaning activity across whole premises and the ordinary spaces that support them; specialised cleaning work is outside that definition. That distinction preserves the character of the activity as an ongoing operational service for buildings, rather than a label for every cleaning task that might occur at a property.

Registration is available at Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scale. Nationally, the activity is TERBUKA to PMA, with foreign ownership permitted up to 100%. In other words, the national position does not impose a foreign-equity cap below full ownership for this activity. The relevant national reference is Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. For a founder considering the activity at national level, the picture is therefore straightforward: it is open to foreign-investment registration across the listed business scales.

Bali is the decisive exception. A foreigner cannot register this activity through PMA in Bali today. At the Besar scale, every scope is assessed in OSS as Rendah or Menengah-Rendah risk, which brings the activity within Bali’s moratorium dated May 13, 2026. The block is island-wide and permanent under the stated Bali rule. A national 100% ceiling does not overcome Bali’s island-wide, permanent block on PMA registration for this activity. The honest reading is not that Bali applies a lower foreign-ownership percentage; it is that PMA registration for this activity is blocked there despite the nationally open position.
